title: 2026/08/20 - EN (Part 2 of 2)
machineSummary: Submitters Forest and Bird, Tourism Industry Aotearoa, and Recreation Aotearoa debated the Conservation Amendment Bill. Forest and Bird said it should be binned unless economic clauses are removed, citing Denniston Plateau, $19 billion tourism, and $300 million subsidies. TIA and Recreation Aotearoa urged DOC concession and levy reforms.

To start, because we have limited time. So, we're back into public submissions on the Conservation Amendment Bill, and our first submitter this afternoon is Forest and Bird. Welcome to the select committee. We're looking forward to your submission. We have 15 minutes with you, so we'll hand it over to you

to open up, but take your submission as read, and then we'll open up for questions. So over to you. Thank you. Tena koutou katoa. Thank you, Chair and committee members for the opportunity to appear today. My name's Erika Tolman. I'm the acting CE. With me is Richard Kape, GM Policy and Advocacy, and online is Tim Williams, our senior environmental lawyer.

As most of you know, Forest and Bird is New Zealand's largest independent conservation organization. For more than 100 years, we've worked across New Zealand's unique natural heritage. We represent New Zealanders from across the motu. And our history includes the founding and development of New Zealand's conservation system, including the part we played in the establishment of the current Conservation Act.

So before turning to the detail of our submission, I want to make Forest and Bird's overall position clear. If this bill cannot be fixed, particularly proposed Section 6EA and its counterparts, the visitor amenity areas, and the conservation planning processes, this bill should not proceed. While we recognize the need for some reform to ease DOC's administrative burden, reform cannot proceed on the basis set out in this bill.

Unless significant changes are made, Forest and Bird says this bill should be binned. So, the Conservation Act exists because Parliament recognized that public conservation land needs a clear legal framework focused on protection. That framework is not anti-tourism or necessarily anti-use. It already allows appropriate use where it's consistent with conservation.

But it's not an economic development statute, and DOC should not be turned into an economic development agency. Conservation land and the nature within it is already under considerable pressure. Native biodiversity continues to decline. Thousands of species are threatened or at risk, and many ecosystems are still deteriorating.

It would be unthinkable and wrong in that context to weaken the legal framework that protects the places those species depend on. Now, New Zealanders have made clear that public conservation land should not be sold, swapped, or opened up for development. Strong conservation safeguards and conservation supremacy must remain central to our approach.

I want to acknowledge the government's commitment to removing the exchange and disposal provisions from the bill, and to retain the existing provisions in the Conservation Act, so that conservation land will not be opened up for disposal unless the land has no or low conservation values. But to maintain that current approach to exchange and disposal under the Act, the government will also need to fix the economic use and development provisions, and to remove the backdoor for conservation land disposal in the Fast Track

Act. So, we're going to cover four key matters in our remarks today, and I'll start off with proposed Section 6EA and its counterparts. So, our most significant concern, is the proposed Section 6EA, together with the equivalent references in the proposed purpose provisions for the NCPS in Section 13D, for area plans, Section 13H, and concessions, Section 141.

As drafted, that section would require DOC to recognize economic opportunities and enable economic use and development of public conservation land to the greatest extent practicable. The problem is not that economic activity happens on conservation land. It already does. The problem is making economic development a statutory objective in its own right, rather than something that's only allowed where it's consistent with conservation.

So it's not a small administrative change. It is a fundamental change that would change the legal starting point for all future decisions under the Act. It would materially change conservation in New Zealand. It would also make disposal of public conservation land easier in both the declassification decisions and exchange decisions.

It would make it easier for mining on PCL to happen. So our strongly preferred position is that 6 A is deleted. However, if the committee would like to include it, we've included wording in our submission for it to be amended. And I'd just reiterate that it's not just 6 A, that it does feature in several other parts of the bill.

Turning then to the backdoor Fast Track Approvals Act process. So I want to make it really clear today that even if the exchange and dispose provisions are removed from the bill, the protection for conservation land that New Zealanders have demanded will not be achieved unless the Fast Track Act is also changed.

The reason is straightforward. The Fast Track Act creates a pathway for disposal by exchange of large amounts of public conservation land, which is the same outcome that New Zealanders loudly opposed earlier this year. So first off, the Fast Track Act roughly doubles the amount of land available for disposal by exchange. So under the Conservation Act currently, it's only stewardship land is potentially available.

Under the Fast Track Act, a much broader range of conservation land classifications is available other than very highly protected land like the national parks. Secondly, under the Fast Track Act, its own test is included for exchanges. So it's different from the Conservation Act test, and it's much less protective.

And part of that is that the environmental values of the exchange land don't need to reflect a net gain for biodiversity, because money that DOC gets as part of the exchange can also be considered in the weighing up. So New Zealanders have made their feelings clear that conservation land should not be disposed of, and fixing this bill alone will not address those concerns.

The Fast Track Approvals Act must also be amended so that the regime is subject to the status quo measures under the Conservation Act that the government has promised to preserve. So this is available to the committee, that this bill already makes changes to the Fast Track Approvals Act, and we've set out in our submission the exact changes that are needed that the government can make good on its promise in respect to conservation land.

Turning now to exchange and disposal. So while the government has made a commitment to remove those provisions, which we support, we are aware that there's still a wish to be able to address what the minister has called bits and bobs. As we've said repeatedly, when discussing the likes of the offsite MetService building, we are not outright opposed to the sale or exchange of conservation land where the land has no or very low conservation value.

But we say that before designing any mechanism to dispose of conservation land, we have to be really clear on what the policy problem is that we're trying to solve and not rely on anecdotes. We have not seen that clear problem statement set out. We're very willing to work with ministers and the department, once that statement is made really clear.

If any changes are needed to those provisions, they must be very tightly designed. Only land with no or very low conservation value should be considered. Conservation values must be assessed robustly, and approval should be recommended through an independent mechanism, such as the NZCA, rather than left to broad ministerial discretion.

I'll pass now to my colleague, Richard. Thanks, Erica. Kia ora, everybody. It's nice to see you all again. There's several other points that might not have received the same amount of attention as, say, disposals or 6 A economic development, but which are actually really significant, and I think it's important to briefly put those before the committee. So the first thing I really want to reiterate is that stewardship land is conservation land.

That is how it is categorized under law. So the assessment and reclassification process for stewardship land must be completed so that the conservation values of those lands are properly protected and genuinely low-value lands can be dealt with transparency. As a very live and real example, I would draw your attention to the very threat that exists just now around one of New Zealand's national treasures, the Denniston Plateau.

Mm. The Denniston Plateau should be a scientific reserve. The evidence is very clear that that is the status that it should hold. That would make it protected under Schedule 4, and it would not be possible to mine that. Instead, New Zealand faces the very real prospect of that wonderful place being ripped apart for an opencast coal mine.

This needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency. The other thing that I think we need to think about in the context of this bill is the centralization of power. We are in favor of administrative processes being streamlined, but I think as we've seen around the Fast Track Act and many of the discussions that are happening very live just now, whether it's in Orewa, Pegasus, Fernhill, Arrowtown, Devonport, New Zealanders want their local voices heard.

So taking local voices and independent checks out of the conservation system is something that we strongly oppose. Government should retain meaningful decision-making and the oversight roles of conservation boards and the New Zealand Conservation Authority rather than reducing them to be advisory bodies.

Ministerial powers need to be constrained, and they should be constrained by clear statutory criteria and conservation purposes. That avoids political flip-flopping, decision-making made in political cycles, and therefore provides certainty and clarity not only to the conservation system, but to businesses and commercial operators who want to operate within conservation With regards visitor amenity areas, better visitor infrastructure may be appropriate, but the current provisions in this bill are too permissive. They risk undermining the very reasons, the very

values, why people come to these places in the first place. Government should strengthen the test that amenities could not be located reasonably outside conservation land, and make this a key consideration. So why are we looking to locate these amenities in the conservation land when we could actually be supporting regional economies and local towns by requiring that those amenities are located in those spaces? There is a missed opportunity here.

On concessions and the National Conservation Policy Statement, DOC is currently consulting on a draft of the first of these policy statements. The proposed economic use and development provisions in this bill have actually resulted in that draft, which is inconsistent with the Conservation Act, and any concessions framework needs to be consistent with conservation. The draft NCS would attempt to, for example, deem hydro schemes as being consistent with the purposes for which conservation parks are held.

That's wrong, and it would create clear conflicts and inefficiencies for DOC processes instead of actually achieving the ambition of this bill, which is modernization and streamlining. Government should remove the economic development objective and function from the bill, ensure that the new planning framework for conservation has conservation as its clear primary purpose.

So the NCPS was launched in parallel with this bill, and I think the intention was to enable people to be able to read them side by side. The unfortunate consequence of that is because of the significant flaws in this bill, the NCPS now needs to be withdrawn and rewritten. So it's significantly flawed, and actually the interaction of the two means that we need to start again on the NCPS.

Finally, we'd ask the committee not to weaken the existing treaty obligations or reduce the formal channels through which tangata whenua perspectives are brought into conservation planning. And you shouldn't look to weaken Section 4 or existing treaty obligations. I think we're seeing the incredible value that mana whenua are bringing to understanding conservation of place, and removing those contributions would be a very bad move.

Look, finally, I note we are not opposed in principle to reasonable access charges. So charging international visitors to access the conservation estate, we don't have a problem with. But I think we've also got to be clear, it would be additional to DOC's core funding, and there should be transparency dedicated to conservation, visitor infrastructure, biodiversity, and heritage outcomes.

I think in making that point, I think Forest and Bird is acutely aware that you may be-- one of the main arguments that we've heard is that we need to generate more revenue for conservation land. And we think appropriate revenue tools can be part of the solution, but you don't redefine the purpose of the conservation estate in order to do that.

I think it's also important to point out just how much value the conservation estate already delivers to New Zealanders, and we heard this in that outpouring of aroha and that outpouring of emotion from so many people across the country when we produced those maps. The amount of return that we get from the conservation estate massively outweighs the meager funding it receives.

So we know tourism alone is worth $19 billion to New Zealand this year, and the tourists do not come here for our shopping malls. There are also funding choices that we can make. Government is currently spending $100 million of taxpayers' money on supporting mining companies and another $200 million of taxpayer money for fossil fuel exploration.

That is $300 million, or 40% of DOC's annual budget. There are choices that we can make. So just round off our comments, um- You actually have about a minute for questions, so just- Okay. I will say no more. And we have got questions, and members, if we can keep them tight.

So, Priyanka. Yes. Okay, so this is about enabling more economic development on public conservation land. You've talked about the removal of the sale and exchange clauses from the bill and ensuring that the primary objective of DOC remains conservation. Is that enough to protect public conservation land?

No, quite frankly, and Forest and Bird really grappled with should we advocate for getting rid of this whole bill, because there are serious problems with it. However, we do recognize that DOC needs to relieve their burden, so we are not quite at the point of saying bin the bill yet, on the proviso that these changes that we've set out, as well as the changes to the Fast-track Approvals Act, can be made.

Thank you. Grant? Yeah, and carrying on, on that theme around economic development. So how do you address the issue that came up when Cathedral Cove was shut for nearly two years? The local businesses in Hahei basically lost all-- their patronage went down. They really, really struggled. Mm-hmm. And DOC basically said, "Well, it's not our job to worry about the local economy." How do you balance that given the reason they were coming there was to go across to Cathedral Cove?

Excuse me, my nose is running. Oh. Carry on. Yes, please. So I'm happy to talk to this one. So again, that goes back to my point there. So we're defunding DOC. So DOC's budget is being cut year on year, and it's got a massive budget shortfall forecast for the next few years. But as you said, Grant, the amount of value that DOC delivers to our local communities, to our country, and our economy as a whole is significant. Part of the reason that I imagine it was saying that we can't do this is it didn't have the money.

Mm-hmm. So if you actually fund DOC properly- Then actually its ability to support and expand that kind of local economic benefits is there. But you do not need to change that act in order to do that. You just need to get those funding settings right. Okay. Thank you. One last question. I wanted to pick up, there's so much in here, particularly about the ministerial boards. What would be your main concerns about that change from the conservation boards in particular, and the New Zealand Conservation Authority to ministers? What's your main concerns with that?
Tim, do you want to answer that one?

Sure. I think it's probably the point that Richard already made, which is that it's really important to be able to have a consistent conservation focused approach to this, and when you put too much power in the hands of the ministers, it just results in shorter term decision making and, essentially decision making that isn't focused on conservation. So, having independent expert bodies that can direct actions towards the purpose of the act is a really important feature.

Look, thank you very much. We have gone over time, but look, we do really respect the work that you put onto this, all the valuable feedback that you're giving us, and we really appreciate that. So thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. We now call upon our next submitter, who is Tourism Industry Aotearoa.

Thank you. Welcome to the select committee this afternoon. You have 15 minutes with us, so we'll pass it over to you to make your introductions. Thank you. And then open up for questions. Thank you. Kia ora chair and committee. Thank you very much for inviting Tourism Industry Aotearoa to submit for you in person today.

I am Rebecca Ingram, the chief executive of Tourism Industry Aotearoa. We have approximately 1,200 tourism businesses who are our members. That stretches from everything from Kapiti Island Nature Tours through to Air New Zealand. Tourism and conservation are deeply connected.

New Zealand's natural environment is the foundation of many visitors' experiences, and tourism operators have a strong interest in tourism and conservation working well together, and conservation being protected and enhanced. Retaining the status quo is not our preferred option.

We strongly support the direction of the reform. Our submission is about getting the system settings right. There are three areas I would like to focus on today. Our first concern is the proposed function requiring the department to enable use and development to the greatest extent.

We think the wording in the bill goes too far. It potentially creates uncertainty about whether economic development is being elevated above conservation outcomes. Our preferred wording is simple. DOC should enable use and development to the extent consistent with conservation.

Making this change will give DOC a clear and positive mandate to recognize and enable appropriate economic development and tourism opportunities while establishing a clear conservation boundary. This balance is something the legislation must strike. With regard to concessions and investment certainty, TIA strongly supports the intent of modernizing concessions.

Our comments relate to concession system, both in terms of how the concessions are granted and how competitive allocation will work. For a tourism operator, a concession is often the cornerstone of their business. It allows them to invest in facilities, people and systems.

Many concessionaires have spent decades developing operations around particular places, and are genuine partners in conservation efforts. They invest in predator control, restoration projects, visitor education, yet the current framework can feel more transactional than collaborative.

Here is an example of how the current system can play out for a tourism business. We have a TIA member that has been operating responsibly on PCL for almost 40 years, including making a significant contribution to conservation. Following the process outlined by DOC, they applied to renew their concession when it was due to expire in 2023.

DOC initially offered a concession that in some cases reduced their allocation by over 90%, completely devaluing their business. It then took two and a half years to prove their case, which highlighted inconsistencies in interpretation of planning documents, and the allocation of concessions to other operators. They were finally granted their satisfactory concession in June this year.

While individuals within the department, and I want to make this clearly, were genuinely sympathetic and helpful, they were at the mercy of a broken system that was disempowering businesses and frustrating DOC. For this reason, gains around efficiency, statutory time frames, and improvements to granting processes are very much supported.

With regard to competitive allocation, we acknowledge that competition may be entirely appropriate in some circumstances But operators need clarity about when competitive allocation might occur, how existing investment and conservation contributions will be recognised. That certainty is critical to continued investment and visitor experiences on conservation land, and we therefore ask the committee to recommend greater clarity in the bill around competitive allocation.

We have similar feedback around pre-approved concessions. We support the principle. Removing unnecessary bureaucracy for straightforward, low impact activities does make sense, but the design needs appropriate safeguards. In particular, the 12 month approval may be too short to justify meaningful investment in staff, equipment, safety systems, and product quality.

There's a risk that a mechanism designed to make the system easier could inadvertently favor short term, low investment operators over businesses committed to a place for a long time. There are also questions around cumulative effect, carrying capacity, and how pre-approved activities will interact with existing concessionaires.

My third area of focus is the proposed international visitor access levy. Tia supports the principles, but our support comes with some conditions. First, the revenue should be additional to existing DOC funding. It should not simply substitute Crown funding. Oh.

Second, we believe there should be a very strong connection between where the money is raised and the place that it's collected. Mm-hmm. So if a visitor is being charged for access to a place, they should be able to see their contribution improving conservation and the visitor experience at place. And third, implementation needs to consider how tourism is sold.

Our submission therefore recommends at least 18 months notice before a new access charge takes effect, so operators can incorporate it into their pricing and international contracts if needed. We also need to consider the cumulative cost to the visitor rather than looking at each charge in isolation.

An international visitor already pays, many of them, $100 in the international visitor levy. They may also face parking charges, and costs passed through from other concessionaires. An additional access charge needs to be considered as part of the overall visitor experience. Finally, excuse me.

Many of the practical effects of this legislation will be determined by the policy statement, area plans, and visitor amenity areas, and through future regulations. We support tourism and recreation being explicitly recognized within the new planning framework. Not every operational detail should be in primary legislation, but Parliament does need to establish the important principles and guardrails now.

We also think appropriate scrutiny and recommendation roles remain important, particularly given the greater concentration of decision making authority proposed within the bill. Tia strongly supports modernization of the conservation system. Mm-hmm. We want a system that's easier to navigate, provides certainty, encourages responsible investment, and enables tourism to contribute more to conservation.

This bill should proceed with changes. Three things are fundamental. Conservation must remain the overriding purpose while enabling economic development. The concession system must provide sufficient certainty to encourage long-term investment, and the new powers, planning processes, and visitor charging mechanisms need some statutory guardrails.

With those settings right, we believe this bill can deliver better outcomes for conservation, visitors, tourism businesses, and New Zealand. Thank you. I welcome your questions. Oh. Thank you. Very useful information. Priyanka? Thank you for that.

You shared an example of- Yes... a member who had their concession, renewed but their allocation cut by a significant amount. Took a long time to get reinstated. You made the point that DOC staff were willing to, were sympathetic to the cause. You kind of put it down to time frames, I think, in the existing legislation. I'm assuming there's more to it than that.

Would you be able to expand on what led to that situation- Mm-hmm... in existing leg versus how the proposed changes would alleviate that? Sure. So that is an example. What the existing framework does is it has multiple layers of structures that need to be applied in order for a concession to be delivered.

So you've got conservation management plans, conservation boards. They are sometimes out of date. They haven't recognized what's happening at a place today, and they're all laddering up to a piece of legislation that's almost 40 years old. Yeah. And so the streamlining that will exist in here for concessions in particular will enable DOC to approach standard concessions, and also those concessions where they are with a reputable, well-known established tourism operator to be recognized.

And so the challenge we've got in the way that it works currently is that there's no certainty or consistency in the way that it's applied. And so that's what we're hoping to change through this modernization of the legislation. Thank you. Look, I'm going to go to Rachel online because she didn't get a question before and had her hand up. There you go, Rachel.

Hey. Thank you. Thank you. Hello, everyone. Rob Kneeden here. Hey, um Your experience with the visitor levy, and it's obviously gone up substantially, but our observation is, well, some of us haven't seen that really go into conservation or tourism uses. Instead, it's been used for some other things like advertising to Australia.

If it went up further, do you have ideas of how it could be constrained so that it was actually used on tourism infrastructure and conservation? Sure. So the international visitor levy at $100 per person for most international visitors coming into the country is split in two.

Our position on the IVL is that it should be used 100% for incremental gain and not be used as a substitution for Crown funding. The way in which it is then invested by DOC and through tourism really needs to go into tourism-related infrastructure, amenities.

From a department perspective, it's about making sure that the visitor experience and tourism-related assets that they're responsible for can be kept and advanced, that they're safe, that they can respond to being put right when climate change will have an effect on them.

Mm. So we think that's why it's really important to consider the role of the international visitor levy alongside any new access charges together. So this sort of holistic view. It's also why we believe it's incredibly important that there are quite specific parameters around any new access-related fees in this piece of legislation. It's why we want to see if a new fee is introduced, that it will be used at the place where it is being raised.

Mm. And what supplementary just on that, what do you imagine? Can you just give some color to what you're saying about amenity and the tourism facilities that might be needed? Are you talking toilets? What are we talking about? So at the high visitation sites that we're talking about, I think it's about making sure we've got the core infrastructure in place, that there's appropriate roading, parking, that the bridges are being well-maintained and looked after, that the tracks are up to spec. And that's not just for international visitors.

Anyone who is going to visit those sites will benefit from ensuring that that is well looked after. Then in some places, I think, it's about how we can further enhance those places in a way that delivers more in the visitor experience. So for example, how are we partnering with iwi in specific locations to make sure we're telling appropriate stories of those places?

Mm. Mm. How are we connecting our visitors to conservation outcomes at those places, and the difference they might be making through the contribution of their access levy? So, I think that's important. Look, I've just got a quick question that I wanted to jump in with, because it comes back to 6 , which we've spoken about with lots of submitters. But earlier we had RealNZ, they spoke about tourism being included within that definition. You haven't said that.

Is there a reason you feel it captures tourism with the wording that you're saying here? Sure. So, we are suggesting that it changes in the way it's written. We think the greatest extent is too far. We think with other changes, as identified in our submission, that that purpose statement would be effective.

If we can't achieve some of the concession gains, for example, then I think tourism may need to be more clearly articulated. Okay. Yeah, no, that's great. And just one last quick question, Celia. Oh, thank you very much, and thank you, Rachel, for asking one of my questions in a great answer. I was interested in who you think should be required to pay the visitor access levy.

Mm-hmm. Given the IVL doesn't apply to Australians and certain other categories- Mm-hmm... do you think it should be all nationalities? And then another submission talked about if people are on working holidays and/or they're doing conservation work and so on, should they have some kind of concessional allowance?

Mm-hmm. So as proposed, any international visitor would be paying the access levy for a place that they're choosing to frequent or go to, and we think that is appropriate. There will need to be some definitions, though. So for example, a number of tourism businesses might have a working holiday visa holder from overseas who's working in their business for the summer.

We would want them to be exempt, for example. That's just a really practical example. I think what matters a lot is that the international visitors that are being asked to pay the levy can see how it turns up in their experience. Mm. That the toilets are good quality, and they're being looked after. The tracks are well constructed. I think that's essential.

Thank you very much. We have met time. We appreciate your time today- Thank you... that really thorough submission, so thank you. Thank you. It's great. So we now move to our next submitter, Recreation Aotearoa. Welcome to the select committee this afternoon. You have 15 minutes with us, so we'll hand over to you to make your introductions and then open for questions.

Very good. Tena koutou, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for the opportunity to be here to speak to you today. My name is Sarah Murray, and I'm the Chief Executive of Recreation Aotearoa. We are an industry body and professional association for recreation providers across New Zealand, and our mission is Ti Whai Oranga, enhancing wellbeing through recreation.

And we believe that recreation is not a discretionary nice to have, it's a fundamental component of New Zealand's physical and mental health, social cohesion, youth development, and national identity. Central government, through the Department of Conservation, is the largest provider of outdoor recreation opportunities in New Zealand.

Every year, 80% of us visit public conservation lands to walk, tramp, climb, bike, swim, paddle, and enjoy a range of other recreation activities that help us connect with nature The public conservation estate is New Zealand's largest recreation infrastructure network, and as such, DOC plays a critical role in ensuring New Zealanders can access quality outdoor recreation opportunities and connect with our natural environment.

Recreation Aotearoa supports the bill's goal of modernising conservation management. We recognize that parts of the current system are complex, slow, and resource intensive. We support efforts to streamline planning processes, improve concessions administration, and provide greater consistency across the conservation estate.

We also support proposals to create a national conservation policy statement and introduce area plans, noting that these, we believe, need significant amendments as per our submission on the NCPS. What we don't support are reforms that would alter the fundamental purpose of the Conservation Act or the Department of Conservation's role.

The conservation system must be able to respond to changing visitor expectations, increasing participation in outdoor recreation, growing tourism, and the impacts of climate change. It must also uphold the Crown's obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi and actively support mana whenua to exercise kaitiakitanga.

But modernization of the legislation should improve how the system works, not change why it exists. As currently drafted, the bill shifts the longstanding statutory balance within New Zealand's conservation framework. It fundamentally changes the purpose of conservation land. We strongly oppose the so-called economic clauses, specifically the inclusion of the words "enabling economic activity to the greatest extent practicable" as a key function of the Department of Conservation and as a key purpose of the proposed NCPS area plans and

concessions framework. We acknowledge that economic activity occurs on public conservation land. We're not opposed to this. We support well-managed tourism, and we recognize the important role concessionaires play in helping New Zealanders and visitors access and enjoy public conservation lands. But conservation of our shared natural and historic heritage must remain the primary and overriding purpose of public conservation land, and recreation must continue to be recognized and fostered as a core public benefit, with economic activity enabled only where it

is consistent with conservation and recreation outcomes. As such, we urge the committee to recommend that the existing hierarchy within the act is preserved and that all references to economic activity are qualified with a clear statement requiring consistency with conservation outcomes. Our next point is where we believe the committee has the greatest opportunity to make a practical and meaningful improvement to the bill, and that's around the current treatment of not-for-profit outdoor education providers under the concessions regime.

The way that these providers are currently treated is inequitable and inconsistent. At present, and rightly so, schools can take students onto public conservation land without requiring a concession or incurring the costs and administrative challenges that come with this. However, not-for-profit outdoor education providers delivering the same activities to the same students and tertiary institutions who are training our future recreation, conservation, tourism, and outdoor education workforce, they are required to hold a

concession. The activities are the same, the students are the same, the public good, the public benefit is the same, only the provider differs. In our view, that makes little sense. Outdoor education is an integral part of New Zealand's education system. Going on a school camp, doing your first overnight tramp, crossing a river, visiting a national park for the first time, these are rites of passage for young people in New Zealand.

They're the experiences that help us build resilience, they teach leadership and teamwork, and they build environmental awareness, and oftentimes, they help us develop our sense of identity. Outdoor education connects young people with the natural environment, and it fosters a lifelong love of conservation and recreation. The public conservation estate is also New Zealand's greatest outdoor classroom.

And these days, outdoor education activities are often delivered by specialist outdoor education providers, the vast majority of which are charitable trusts and not-for-profit incorporated societies. Schools often lack the skills, equipment, safety management systems, and experience to deliver outdoor education safely themselves, and these providers are a critical part of the system.

The way that the concessions framework is currently applied to these organizations is inconsistent with the purpose of this part of the act and also with Parliament's original intent when the concessions regime was introduced through the 1996 Conservation Amendment Act, a very similar process to the one that we are in now.

The purpose of the 1996 amendment was to create a consistent and rational approach for regulating commercial activities and business use on conservation land. And commercial activities were defined in the legislation and continue to be defined in the legislation as activities undertaken for gain or reward, pecuniary or otherwise. Not-for-profit charitable organizations delivering outdoor education activities are not commercial businesses.

They do not make a profit, and they do not receive gain or reward from public conservation land. We assert that Parliament did not set out to regulate charitable trusts taking students on their first overnight tramp, yet that is what has happened. The legislation that is intended to foster appreciation and enjoyment of New Zealand's wild places is instead making it harder for young New Zealanders to access, experience, and benefit from them. And this is something that we believe is deeply counterproductive.

This committee has the opportunity to correct this through this bill The bill provides for the minister to classify activities as exempt from the concessions regime. We ask the committee to recommend that outdoor education activities undertaken by not-for-profit outdoor education providers and tertiary institutes be added to the list of activities that can be carried out without a concession in Section 14A of the bill. We also ask that Section 13E explicitly states that the National Conservation Policy Statement must classify outdoor education activities

undertaken by not-for-profit providers as exempt. Those two things are required to give clarity and certainty. We also ask that Section 14A is broadened to make it really clear that cost recovery charges made by not-for-profit providers delivering education activities are not gain or reward.

This would prevent these providers from being misclassified, as they currently are, as businesses simply because they charge to cover gear, staffing, and instructor costs. Relying on interpretation or ministerial discretion alone provides insufficient long-term certainty for the outdoor education sector.

Clear statutory direction is needed to address this inequity and ensure young people continue to have opportunities to take part in outdoor education on public conservation land, regardless of who is running that activity. My final point concerns access charging. system. We also ask the committee to take this opportunity to address the longstanding inequity faced by not-for-profit outdoor education providers.
